en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Resolute Mind, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Buddha...
He addressed Ānanda:

"I am now in meditative concentration, feeling compassion for those in the world who do not know that the Buddha-way is truly vast and profound, yet who, with shallow, false, and frivolous words, wish to harbor jealousy and slander the root of the Way, falsely raising endless challenges against my disciples."
"You should maintain a correct mind and recognize this sinner as either a malevolent sorcerer or an evil teacher, or perhaps a worldly person of deceit who lacks understanding.

If there are bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who are erudite in the scriptures, lofty and pure, and capable of enlightening the ignorant and dark-minded by explaining how the retributions of sin and merit accumulate within birth and death—if such persons can immediately understand and submit themselves to the truth of the Way, they are individuals for whom sin is extinguished and merit is born."

If one explains the Dharma as clearly as pointing at one's own palm or palm of the hand, yet the person’s mind remains muddled and they have no desire to hear it—even if they force themselves to listen, their mind is full of drowsiness;

or if they ruin the Way and its teachings, disparage śramaṇas and upāsakas, and speak with foul mouths and falsehoods—one should recognize that such a person is dragged away by their own transgressions.

O worthy śramaṇa, one who takes patience as primary should be like clear water: there is nothing it will not cleanse—whether a dead person, a dead dog, a dead snake, or excrement and urine—and yet it does not lose its clarity.

One should likewise maintain the mind like a broom sweeping the ground; whether it be clean or unclean, a dead person, a dead dog, a dead snake, or excrement and urine, it sweeps them all away without damaging the broom itself.

Furthermore, it would likewise blow away and burn corpses, dead dogs, dead snakes, excrement, and urine by the power of its wind and fire and the force of its light; yet it would not destroy the power of that wind and fire, nor its light.
If someone comes intending to kill one, one does not become angry;
if they come intending to slander one, one does not become angry;
if they come intending to calumniate one, one does not become angry.
If others wish to come and mock me, I shall not become angry;
if they wish to come and destroy me, preventing me from serving the Buddha-Dharma, I shall likewise not become angry.

One should simply maintain a mind of loving-kindness and right intention; thus, transgressions will be extinguished and blessings will arise, the heterodox will not enter the orthodox, and all evils will be dissolved and decayed.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are those with good hearts and virtuous intentions who, upon hearing the Buddha’s clear Dharma, listen with single-minded attention, they may be able to do so for one day;
if they cannot do so for one day, they may be able to do so for half a day."
If one cannot do it for half a day, one may do it for a single hour;
if one cannot do it for a single hour, one may do it for half an hour;
if one cannot do it for half an hour, one may do it for a brief moment.
The merit thereof is immeasurable and beyond calculation.

"You should extensively expound this for the assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the lay populace; you should also extensively explain the practice of giving, which plants the seeds for the provisions of saṃsāra."

On days of fasting, they prepared meals and invited the fourfold assembly—those learned in the sublime sutras, sages, śramaṇas, and practitioners—to assemble. They prepared high seats for them to discourse upon and expound the Buddhist scriptures, burning incense and lighting lamps whose radiance reached the heavens.
The various devas rejoiced and laughed, all descending from the void to listen with bated breath; there was none who did not feel delighted.

Those who break through stinginess and practice giving for the sake of merit will have benevolent spirits descend immediately to protect their households, warding off calamities and extinguishing portents of misfortune. They shall emerge to meet with profit, and such profit brings auspiciousness; in the end, they shall never encounter resentment or evil.

It is like sowing grain: it grows according to what is sown. By sowing good, one obtains blessings; by sowing evil, one reaps calamity. There has never been one who obtained fruit without having sown.
You should thus rectify your mind, and blessings will naturally accrue to you. Be careful not to consult diviners, lest you be led astray by the heterodox;
if your heart harbors doubt, benevolent spirits will distance themselves from you, and as you constantly enter the realm of sin, whatever you do will not succeed.
They do not realize they have violated the precepts, but instead resent the Buddha and the deities; their service yields no benefit, and thus they fail to rectify their minds.
Whether men or women, there are none who, upon hearing this sutra and upholding, reciting, or reading it, do not obtain merit.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ānanda rejoiced and rose to prostrate before the Buddha.
This concludes the *Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Resolute Mind*.
